title: Cap. 7 Contra Sol. 4: three reasons; Rupertus and Ambrose
latin: Respondeo, ubi de facto aliquo Divino constat, temerarium est (ne dicam impium) de aequitate aut congruitate ejusdem dubitare. Jam vero Christi morte esse stabilitum illud pactum cum humano genere, ex cujus tenore vita aeterna cuivis homini sub Fidei conditione promittitur, jam pridem a nobis demonstratum est. De hoc pacto Rupertus, in 4. Genes. cap. 34, Dicimus pactum multoties quidem promissum, sed semel initum, quo solo inimicitiae solvuntur, quae erant inter Deum & homines, passio scilicet Christi Filii Dei. Illic enim absque ulla contradictione certa est constitutio pacis, dum accepta Deus Fide hominum dat hominibus eundem Christum Filium suum, ut salventur per ipsum. De hac itaque Dei ordinatione in Christi morte meritisque fundata, atque ad omnes & singulos spectante, non est ambigendum. Verum illud adhuc in dubium vocatur, utrum posito hoc universali pacto dandae vitae aeternae omnibus, si crediderint, Deus exerceat libertatem, & exserat specialem misericordiam in danda hac Fide salutifera electis qua credant; idque per Christum, & propter merita Christi peculiari quodam privilegio ad eos applicata. Res ipsa loquitur. Videmus enim electos, & solos electos, in eventu obtinere a Deo fidem perseverantem & salutiferam: Putare autem tantum ac tale donum illis specialiter donatum alio modo, aut intuitu quam propter merita Christi illis speciali quadam intentione Dei ordinata & applicata, plane nefas est. Nam, ut pie Ambrosius, Omne donum gratiae in Christo est, ad illud Apostoli, Ephes. i. 3. Benedixit nobis omni benedictione spirituali in Christo. Hisce constitutis, quamvis (ut dixi) supervacaneum est de congruitate Divinorum factorum disceptare ubi de ipsis factis constat, tamen, ne quid scrupuli relinquatur, primo dicimus, Hanc specialem Dei intentionem, juxta quam apud se decrevit propter merita Christi dare electis specialia beneficia gratiae efficacis & salutis, non pugnare cum pacto illo conditionato, Quisquis crediderit salvus erit, sed potius esse speciale quoddam consilium, ad universalis hujus pacti infallibilem impletionem subordinatum. Qui enim suo arbitrio committuntur sub quibusvis gratiae adminiculis, aut Fidem repellunt, aut excutiunt. Ne itaque pactum illud universale nemini effectum salutis apportaret, Deus speciali hac & arcana sua intentione curavit aliquibus applicatum iri mortis Christi meritum, ad Fidei vitaeque aeternae infallibilem consecutionem. Secundo, dicimus, Nihil iniqui aut incongrui esse, quod haec specialis intentio de efficaci applicatione meritorum Christi in aliquibus, non in omnibus vim suam exserat; quia cum mors Christi sit gratuitum Dei donum humano generi impensum, libera distributio & applicatio meritorum inde redundantium omni jure ex mera Dei voluntate dependere debeat. Tertio, & illud addimus, Deum, qui in Evangelio promisit omnibus & singulis vitam aeternam propter merita Christi, si crediderint, nulli tamen infidelium promisisse se illi propter merita Christi daturum ut infallibiliter & perseveranter credat. Quaero igitur, Ex qua parte versatur haec incongruitas? Non ex parte credentium & servatorum: Nam dare propter merita Christi singularibus personis quod illis singulariter minime promissum fuit, non est culpandae iniquitatis, sed celebrandae bonitatis. Non ex parte incredulorum & perditorum: Nam illud beneficium negare alicui, quod constat te nulla ratione illi debere, nec in se iniquum, nec summae bonitati Divinae incongruum judicari potest.
pass_a_gloss: I answer: where some Divine fact is established, it is rash (not to say impious) to doubt concerning the equity or fittingness of the same. Now that by Christ's death that pact with the human race has been established, from whose tenor eternal life is promised to any human being under the condition of Faith, has long since been demonstrated by us. Concerning this pact Rupertus, in Genesis book 4, chapter 34: We say a pact many times indeed promised, but once entered, by which alone the enmities which were between God and human beings are loosed, namely the passion of Christ the Son of God. For there without any contradiction the constitution of peace is certain, while God, faith of human beings having been accepted, gives to human beings the same Christ his Son, that they may be saved through him. Concerning this ordination of God therefore, founded in Christ's death and merits, and looking to all and each, there is not to be ambiguity. But that is still called into doubt, whether, this universal pact of giving eternal life to all if they have believed having been posited, God exercises liberty and puts forth special mercy in giving this saving Faith to the elect by which they believe; and that through Christ, and on account of Christ's merits applied to them by a certain peculiar privilege. The matter itself speaks. For we see the elect, and the elect alone, in the event obtain from God persevering and saving faith: But to think so great and such a gift specially gifted to them in another way, or with another regard, than on account of Christ's merits ordained and applied to them by a certain special intention of God, is plainly unlawful. For, as Ambrose piously says, Every gift of grace is in Christ, at that saying of the Apostle, Ephesians 1:3: He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. These things having been established, although (as I said) it is superfluous to dispute about the fittingness of Divine deeds where the deeds themselves are established, yet, lest any scruple be left, first we say that this special intention of God, according to which he decreed with himself on account of Christ's merits to give the elect the special benefits of efficacious grace and salvation, does not fight with that conditioned pact, Whoever has believed will be saved, but rather is a certain special counsel subordinated to the infallible fulfillment of this universal pact. For those who are committed to their own choice under whatever helps of grace either repel Faith or shake it off. Lest therefore that universal pact should bring the effect of salvation to no one, God by this special and secret intention of his cared that the merit of Christ's death should be applied to some, unto the infallible obtaining of Faith and eternal life. Second, we say that there is nothing unjust or incongruous in that this special intention concerning the efficacious application of Christ's merits puts forth its force in some, not in all; because since Christ's death is a free gift of God expended on the human race, the free distribution and application of the merits overflowing thence ought by every right to depend on the mere will of God. Third, we also add that God, who in the Gospel promised to all and each eternal life on account of Christ's merits if they have believed, yet promised to none of the unbelieving that he would give to him on account of Christ's merits that he should believe infallibly and perseveringly. I ask therefore, From which side does this incongruity turn? Not from the side of believers and the saved: For to give on account of Christ's merits to singular persons what was least singularly promised to them is not of blameworthy injustice, but of goodness to be celebrated. Not from the side of the unbelieving and the lost: For to deny to someone that benefit which it is established you owe him by no account can be judged neither unjust in itself nor incongruous with the highest Divine goodness.
pass_b: I answer: once a Divine fact stands, it is rash — not to say impious — to quarrel with its equity or fittingness. We have long shown that by Christ's death that covenant with the human race was fixed, by whose terms eternal life is promised to anyone under the condition of faith. On that covenant Rupert of Deutz (on Genesis 4.34) says: we call it a covenant many times promised but once struck, by which alone the enmities between God and humankind are dissolved — namely the passion of Christ the Son of God. There peace is settled without contradiction when God, receiving human faith, gives people the same Christ his Son that they may be saved through him. So there is no doubt about this Divine ordination, founded in Christ's death and merits and looking to every person. What is still doubted is whether, given this universal covenant of eternal life for all who believe, God may freely show special mercy in giving the elect the saving faith by which they believe — and that through Christ, for his merits applied to them by a peculiar privilege. The fact itself speaks. We see the elect alone, in the outcome, receive from God persevering saving faith. To imagine so great a gift given them in any other way or regard than for Christ's merits, ordained and applied by a special Divine intention, is plainly unlawful. As Ambrose says devoutly, every gift of grace is in Christ — pointing to Ephesians 1:3, He has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ. That settled, though it is needless to debate the fittingness of Divine deeds when the deeds themselves are clear, still, to leave no scruple: first, this special intention by which God decreed, for Christ's merits, to give the elect the special benefits of efficacious grace and salvation does not fight the conditioned covenant Whoever believes will be saved; it is rather a special counsel subordinated to that universal covenant's sure fulfillment. Those left to their own choice under any helps of grace either push faith away or shake it off. Lest that universal covenant bring salvation's effect to no one, God by this special and secret intention saw to it that Christ's death-merit would be applied to some for the sure obtaining of faith and eternal life. Second, nothing unjust or incongruous follows if this special intention of efficacious application of Christ's merits puts forth its force in some, not in all: Christ's death is God's free gift to the human race, so free distribution and application of the overflowing merits ought by every right to hang on God's mere will. Third, God, who in the Gospel promised every person eternal life for Christ's merits if they believe, never promised any unbeliever that for those merits he would make him believe surely and perseveringly. So where is the incongruity? Not on the side of believers and the saved: to give singular persons, for Christ's merits, what was never singularly promised them is not blameworthy injustice but goodness to praise. Not on the side of the unbelieving and lost: to deny someone a benefit you owe him by no title is neither unjust in itself nor unfit for God's highest goodness.

title: Cap. 7 close: sufficient for all, efficacious for elect — Amen
latin: Sit itaque haec totius hujus controversiae De Morte Christi summa & conclusio; Mediatorem Dei ac hominum, Jesum Christum, in foedere illo Evangelico sanciendo, ex cujus tenore omni credenti debetur vita aeterna, nullam partitionem hominum vel discretionem instituisse, ut quenquam dicere possimus a mortis suae beneficio exclusum, si crederet: Atque hoc sensu, suffragantibus Scripturis, Patribus, ac solidis rationibus, tuemur, Christum pro omnibus hominibus, sive pro toto humano genere, in cruce passum ac mortuum fuisse. Quinetiam addimus & hoc, Eundem Mediatorem, cum animam suam pro peccato decrevisset ponere, habuisse insuper hanc singularem intentionem, quod virtute meritorum suorum efficaciter & infallibiliter quosdam sibi a Patre singulariter datos esset vivificaturus & ad vitam perducturus: Atque hoc sensu defendimus, Christum pro solis Electis, vel pro Ecclesia sua acquirenda, animam suam posuisse, id est, pro illis solis mortuum fuisse cum hoc singulari & certo proposito per meritum mortis suae eos efficaciter regenerandi & salvandi. Quamvis ergo meritum Christi aequaliter se habeat ad omnes quoad sufficientiam, non tamen quoad efficaciam: quod intelligendum est non tantum ex parte effectus, qui in uno fit & non in alio, sed etiam ex parte voluntatis, qua ipse Christus meruit, & diverso modo obtulit sua merita pro diversis. Prima autem radix hujus diversitatis fuit electio & voluntas Divina, cui se voluntas humana Christi conformavit. Atque hinc recte deducit Suarez, Meritum hoc Christi esse causam ipsius spiritualis regenerationis, & dare illi efficaciam, & influere in effectum ejus, & simul causam esse ut hic homo regeneretur, propter quem specialiter suum obtulit meritum, In 3. qu. 19. disp. 41. S. 2. pag. 635. Pro nostris loquatur vir eximiae eruditionis & piae memoriae Robertus Sarisburiensis; sic igitur ille, in Thomson. Diatrib. pag. 94. Nos etsi Christum pro omnibus mortuum non negamus, specialiter tamen & proprie credimus mortuum esse pro Ecclesia, neque ad omnes homines beneficium redemtionis pari jure pertinere. Atque ab hujus beneficii proprietate, non ab humana aliquatenus voluntate pendet efficacia mediorum omnium, ut illis tantum sint, & ex usu sint, quos Christus in se electos peculiari quodam intuitu redemit: neque ex eo effectum sortiantur, quia nos volumus, sed ex eo quod in electis & redemtis secundum propositum gratiae suae operatur Deus hoc velle ad quod elegit. Qui igitur morte sua omnibus sufficientissime promeruit vitam aeternam, donandam utique omnibus ex pacto Evangelico, si crederent; is aliquibus ex peculiari meritorum suorum applicatione promeruit efficacissime ut crederent, ut vitam aeternam ex gratuito Dei dono per & propter Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum acciperent. Atque haec est sors electorum peculiaris: Cujus nos omnes participes faciat Pater misericordiarum, cui cum Filio & Spiritu Sancto sit honor, laus & gloria nunc & in secula sempiterna. Amen.
pass_a_gloss: Let this therefore be the sum and conclusion of this whole controversy On the Death of Christ; that the Mediator of God and human beings, Jesus Christ, in establishing that Evangelical covenant, from whose tenor eternal life is owed to every believer, instituted no partition of human beings or discrimination, so that we could say anyone was excluded from the benefit of his death, if he believed: And in this sense, with the Scriptures, Fathers, and solid reasons assenting, we maintain that Christ suffered and died on the cross for all human beings, or for the whole human race. Moreover we also add this, that the same Mediator, when he had decreed to lay down his soul for sin, had besides this singular intention, that by the virtue of his merits he would efficaciously and infallibly vivify and lead to life certain ones singularly given to him by the Father: And in this sense we defend that Christ laid down his soul for the Elect alone, or for acquiring his Church, that is, that he died for them alone with this singular and certain purpose of efficaciously regenerating and saving them through the merit of his death. Although therefore Christ's merit holds itself equally toward all as to sufficiency, yet not as to efficacy: which is to be understood not only from the side of the effect, which happens in one and not in another, but also from the side of the will by which Christ himself merited, and in a diverse manner offered his merits for diverse persons. But the first root of this diversity was Divine election and will, to which Christ's human will conformed itself. And from this Suarez rightly deduces that this merit of Christ is the cause of spiritual regeneration itself, and gives it efficacy, and influences into its effect, and at the same time is the cause that this human being is regenerated, for whom he specially offered his merit, In 3, question 19, disputation 41, section 2, page 635. Let a man of outstanding learning and pious memory, Robert of Salisbury, speak for ours; thus therefore he, in Thomson's Diatribe, page 94: Although we do not deny that Christ died for all, yet we specially and properly believe that he died for the Church, and that the benefit of redemption does not pertain to all human beings by equal right. And on the peculiarity of this benefit, not on the human will to any degree, hangs the efficacy of all the means, so that they are and are of use only for those whom Christ redeemed in himself as elect by a certain peculiar regard: nor do they obtain effect from this, because we will, but from this, that in the elect and redeemed according to the purpose of his grace God works this willing for which he elected. He therefore who by his death most sufficiently merited eternal life for all, to be gifted indeed to all from the Evangelical pact if they believed; he for some by a peculiar application of his merits most efficaciously merited that they should believe, that they should receive eternal life from God's free gift through and on account of our Lord Jesus Christ. And this is the peculiar lot of the elect: Of which may the Father of mercies make us all partakers, to whom with the Son and the Holy Spirit be honor, praise, and glory now and unto everlasting ages. Amen.
pass_b: Let this be the sum and close of the whole controversy On the Death of Christ. The Mediator between God and humankind, Jesus Christ, in sealing that evangelical covenant by which eternal life is due to every believer, made no partition or sorting of people by which we could say anyone was shut out from the benefit of his death if he believed. In that sense — with Scripture, the Fathers, and solid reasons agreeing — we hold that Christ suffered and died on the cross for all human beings, for the whole human race. We add this too: the same Mediator, when he decreed to lay down his life for sin, also had this singular intention — that by the virtue of his merits he would efficaciously and surely vivify and bring to life certain ones singularly given him by the Father. In that sense we defend that Christ laid down his life for the elect alone, or to acquire his Church — that is, he died for them alone with this singular, fixed purpose of efficaciously regenerating and saving them through the merit of his death. So Christ's merit stands equally toward all as to sufficiency, yet not as to efficacy — and that not only from the effect, which lands in one and not another, but from the will by which Christ himself merited and offered his merits in different ways for different people. The first root of that diversity was Divine election and will, to which Christ's human will conformed. From this Suarez rightly draws that this merit of Christ is the cause of spiritual regeneration itself, gives it efficacy, influences its effect, and is at once the cause that this person is regenerated for whom he specially offered his merit (In 3, q. 19, disp. 41, §2, p. 635). Let Robert of Salisbury, of rare learning and pious memory, speak for our side (in Thomson's Diatribe, p. 94): though we do not deny that Christ died for all, yet we specially and properly believe he died for the Church, and that redemption's benefit does not belong to all by equal right. On that benefit's peculiarity — not on human will — hangs the efficacy of every means, so that they are and are useful only for those whom Christ redeemed in himself as elect under a peculiar regard; nor do they take effect because we will, but because in the elect and redeemed, according to the purpose of his grace, God works the willing for which he chose them. He who by his death most sufficiently merited eternal life for all — to be given to all under the evangelical covenant if they believed — also, by a peculiar application of his merits, most efficaciously merited for some that they should believe and receive eternal life as God's free gift through and for our Lord Jesus Christ. That is the elect's peculiar lot. May the Father of mercies make us all partakers of it; to him, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, be honor, praise, and glory now and forever. Amen.
